source.title: SAFR: Neuron Redistribution for Interpretability
source.authors: Ruidi Chang; Chun-Yuan Deng; Hanjie Chen

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether regularization can improve an interpretability proxy using a different method and measure: training with SAFR regularizers and evaluating a capacity-based token deletion score.
record.gate_note: The study tests a single-layer transformer for text classification, not Qwen3 or another large pretrained model. Its SRS is a token-capacity deletion metric, not a count of neuron poles with one or more human-interpretable jobs. It does not test explanations on held-out activations, automated neuron-explanation scores, attribution graphs, or the cited InceptionV1 examples. The paper also reports accuracy after random and capacity-based token deletion, but SRS is the reported interpretability outcome catalogued here.
record.test_reason: Not a test of any version. The study trains a one-layer text classifier with a loss designed to make token representations monosemantic (SAFR), so the behaviour is induced on purpose. Its outcome, SRS, is the accuracy drop after deleting the top-k% tokens ranked by capacity. That is a token-deletion proxy, not a share of interpretable neurons or poles. No pretrained model is audited, no architectures or interpretability tools are compared, and no vision model is studied. V4's claim, that the interpretable-neuron share rises with better tools and architectures, is not measured. The study is SAFR's own method compared with its own baseline. It assumes superposition is common and does not engage the essay.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that SAFR improves interpretability, as measured by their SRS metric, on SST-2 and IMDB without compromising prediction accuracy, and that it provides neuron-allocation visualizations. Two qualifications: 'comparable accuracy' holds only at the selected λ settings, since high λ drops IMDB accuracy to about 52%. The authors also acknowledge that SRS is their own proxy and that more standardized metrics are needed.
record.recipe_differences: SAFR changes the training loss to regularize token-level representations and evaluates a capacity-based token deletion score. It does not use the original audit's neuron-pole explanations or test explanations on held-out activating examples.
record.method_sensitivity: SRS varies with dataset and with λImp and λInter; some high-regularization settings do not exceed the baseline.

fits_no_version.finding: In a one-layer transformer with random embeddings, adding monosemanticity and interaction regularizers raises SRS (a capacity-based token-deletion accuracy drop) from 4.00 to 17.21 on SST-2 and from 3.54 to 28.48 on IMDB. The gain depends on the λ weights. At λ=100 on IMDB, clean accuracy falls to about 52%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training-time regularization toward monosemantic token representations increases a token-deletion interpretability proxy in small transformers, with a λ-dependent accuracy cost.

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The evidence uses a single-layer transformer with random embeddings on two classification datasets. SRS is an indirect token-deletion proxy, not a direct measure of neuron interpretability or pole-level job counts. The authors note that more comprehensive and standardized evaluation metrics are needed, that scalability to more complex architectures is unexplored, and that the causal mechanisms are not fully elucidated. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

untested.parts: No cross-model or scale comparison of interpretable shares.
No InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic neuron analysis.
No measured share of interpretable neurons; no comparison of architectures or tools; regularization is applied to induce monosemanticity, and the outcome is a token-deletion proxy.
No attribution graphs or replacement models.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and its V4 labels should be dropped. SAFR is the study's own method compared with its own baseline, and the behaviour is induced by a training loss. SRS measures accuracy loss after capacity-ranked token deletion, not how many neurons are interpretable. The paper assumes superposition is common and does not address the essay's claims.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B audit or proportions of neuron poles with one job, two jobs, or unknown jobs.
No comparison across language models, dense and mixture-of-experts models, or model scales.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron or test of pose, recursive generalization, or superposition.

Tests the effect of regularization on an interpretability proxy in one single-layer text-classification transformer. Does not compare architectures or tool quality, test vision models, or estimate the share of interpretable neurons.
No attribution graphs or comparison with a trained replacement model.
No explanations tested against activations outside the examples used to form them.
No automated explanation scoring by simulating neuron activations on new text.
